subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Rehana: Jyoti, you're the class rep. can you ask sir to excuse me for Thursday's lab? I was at my Nani's funeral in Kanpur
Jyoti: I'm so sorry, Rehana
Jyoti: I'll pass it on. but the rule is below 75 percent attendance you can't sit the exam
Rehana: I know the rule. I'm asking for one exception
Jyoti: if I push for you, what if everyone breaks the rules with a story?
Rehana: it's not a story. it's my Nani
Jyoti: I know. I'm not saying you're lying
Jyoti: rules only hold the class together if they're the same for everyone
Rehana: so a funeral and a movie count the same?
Jyoti: ...that's not what I mean
Rehana: it's what it feels like
Jyoti: I'll forward your message to sir tonight, word for word
Rehana: fine

qa.q: Why did Rehana miss Thursday's lab?
qa.a: Rehana was at Nani's funeral in Kanpur.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's reply '...that's not what I mean' suggest Jyoti is feeling?
qa.a: Jyoti seems caught off guard and uneasy, sensing that the strict rule treats a funeral like a movie, which Jyoti never intended.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do next that keeps the rule fair and still helps Rehana?
qa.a: Jyoti could forward the request with its reason and ask the teacher whether there is a proper process for bereavement, instead of assuming no exception is possible.

qa.q: What is it like for Rehana to hear 'what if everyone breaks the rules with a story'?
qa.a: Rehana feels a real loss is being treated as a possible excuse, which hurts deeply while grieving.

grounding: A class representative insists rules must be the same for everyone and asks what if everyone broke them, which keeps order but is hard on a grieving classmate.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: The ration shop in Chandpur opened at eight, and by nine the queue curled past the well. Nazia, twenty and three months into her job as the shop's record keeper, kept the register the way she had been trained: every card holder signs for themselves. Bidisha reached the counter holding her grandmother's card. "Thamma can't walk since the fall. I've brought a letter from the pradhan." Nazia's pen stopped. She liked this rule; it had ended the days when grain vanished under other people's names. "If I make one exception, everyone will bring a letter. What if everyone broke the rules? The whole system falls apart." Bidisha's eyes filled. "So she doesn't eat this month?" The people behind shifted and muttered. Nazia looked at the register, then at the letter, and felt the ground under her rule move a little.

qa.q: What did Bidisha bring from the pradhan?
qa.a: A letter.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's pen stop when Bidisha reached the counter?
qa.a: She believed in the rule because it had ended grain vanishing under other names, and she feared one exception would bring everyone with a letter.

qa.q: What could Nazia do next that respects both the rule and Bidisha's grandmother?
qa.a: She could ask her supervisor whether there is an approved way to serve a card holder who cannot walk, instead of refusing outright or bending the register alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Bidisha to hear 'What if everyone broke the rules?'
qa.a: Bidisha feels her grandmother's real need is being treated as a threat to the system, and fears Thamma will go without grain this month.

grounding: A young record keeper defends a strict signing rule as the thing holding the system together, which protects order but is hard on a rare genuine exception.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: At twelve minutes past six the sun dropped behind the hills outside the university library in Cape Town, and Sami unwrapped three dates at a corner desk. Lindiwe, twenty and on her evening shift at the front desk, walked over at once. "Sorry. No food in the reading room. It's on every door." "I've been fasting since dawn," Sami said quietly. "It's three dates. I'll be out of the way." Lindiwe hesitated. She believed in the rule; last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals. "If I let you, the next person brings chips, then pizza. What if everyone broke the rules for their own good reason?" Sami wrapped the dates up again and went outside to eat on the cold steps. Lindiwe returned to the desk and stamped books a little harder than she needed to.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe believe in the no-food rule?
qa.a: Last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe stamping the books harder suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems uneasy, perhaps guilty, about sending a fasting student out to the cold steps, even though she believes she kept the rule.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe have tried that kept the rule's purpose and still helped Sami?
qa.a: She could have pointed Sami to a spot by the entrance or asked a supervisor about a brief allowance, so the shelves stay safe without shutting Sami out.

qa.q: How might Sami see the rule after eating on the cold steps?
qa.a: Sami may feel the rule was applied without seeing a rare, real need, and may feel less welcome in the library.

grounding: A young library assistant defends a no-food rule with 'what if everyone broke the rules', protecting order but treating a rare, genuine need harshly.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
The hostel rule was taped beside the register at the front desk: no visitors in the lobby after eight. At ten past eight, Tejas came in with his grandmother, grey with tiredness from a delayed train.
"Just till my cousin comes to take her," he said. "Forty minutes."
Vinita, twenty, the student desk volunteer that month, didn't even glance at the clock. "I'm sorry. After eight, no visitors."
"She's seventy-three. It's raining."
"If I let her sit, tomorrow everyone's aunt sits, and the day after nobody reads anything on that board. A rule only works if it works for everyone."
Tejas stared at her. His grandmother pulled her shawl tighter. "Come, beta, we'll wait at the tea stall."
Vinita watched them go, her hand flat on the rule sheet, and felt right and a little cold at the same time.

qa.q: What time did Tejas come in with his grandmother?
qa.a: He came in at ten past eight.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel as she watched them leave?
qa.a: She felt right and a little cold at the same time, sure the rule mattered yet uneasy about sending an old woman into the rain.

qa.q: Where was the turning point, and what choice could have kept order and still helped?
qa.a: When Tejas said his grandmother was seventy-three and it was raining; Vinita could have called the warden for a one-time exception noted in the register.

qa.q: How might Tejas see the hostel rules after that night?
qa.a: He may see them as rigid and uncaring, since they left his tired grandmother waiting at a tea stall in the rain.

grounding: A hostel desk volunteer enforces the visitor rule by asking what happens if everyone is let in, keeping order but being hard on a rare case.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Dear Tenzin,
I know you're angry, and I'm writing because I couldn't say this properly in the union office.
When the river flooded your hostel block and your club's receipts went with it, I believed every word. I still do. But as treasurer I can't release the trek money without bills. The rule says no bill, no money, and I signed that I would keep it.
Think about it. If I pay you on trust, next month the dance club will have lost receipts, then the quiz club, and soon the union account is whatever anyone says it is. The rules are the only thing holding that money together for everybody.
I also know this is hard on you. You did nothing wrong. Maybe the shops can reprint the bills? I'll come with you if you want.
Your friend,
Nirmala

qa.q: What happened to the club's receipts?
qa.a: They went with the water when the river flooded Tenzin's hostel block.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels torn, not just strict?
qa.a: Nirmala says Tenzin did nothing wrong, admits the rule is hard on Tenzin, and offers to go to the shops together.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's pay-on-trust argument do well, and where does it fall short?
qa.a: It protects the union's money for every club, but it treats a real flood like any excuse and leaves Tenzin's trek at risk.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin to read this letter after the argument?
qa.a: Tenzin may still feel stuck and angry about the trek, but perhaps less judged, since the letter says plainly that Tenzin is believed.

grounding: A student treasurer holds to the no-bill rule because rules keep order for everyone, while seeing that it is hard on a friend's rare flood case.
